answer.label: Lao Tzu’s chapter — but a named translator’s English
answer.authorDates: fl. 6th century BCE (traditional) · semi-legendary Chinese sage, reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
answer.sourceLine: This is a real rendering of Tao Te Ching chapter 73, not an invented line. The American philosopher Archie J. Bahm (1907–1996) translates the passage: “Nature itself has the patience to endure insult… It does not explain; nevertheless all understand. It does not command; but all eventually obey. It does not hurry; yet everything is accomplished.” The popular quotation is that final sentence with the pronoun resolved to its antecedent four sentences earlier — and Bahm’s name removed.

source.heading: Where the wording really comes from
source.excerpt: “Nature itself has the patience to endure insult, yet always wins in the end. It does not explain; nevertheless all understand. It does not command; but all eventually obey. It does not hurry; yet everything is accomplished.” — Tao Te Ching ch. 73, trans. Archie J. Bahm.
trail: The exact sentence is credited to Lao Tzu across quote sites with no work, chapter, or translator — Goodreads lists it with 1,400+ likes and no source ↗.
Matching the wording against published English versions locates it in Archie J. Bahm’s rendering of chapter 73 — not chapter 37, and not a paraphrase ↗.
The Chinese of ch. 73, 繟然而善謀, is rendered elsewhere as “without haste”, confirming “does not hurry” as an ordinary translation of that phrase rather than an invention.
source.excerptNote: The popular one-liner is Bahm’s last sentence with “It” replaced by its antecedent, “Nature”. Nothing is invented; the translator is simply dropped.

source.rightsNote: The ancient Chinese original is public domain, but rights attach to the exact English wording, and that wording is Archie J. Bahm’s translation, first published 1958. A 1958 US publication can still be in copyright depending on renewal, which we have not established — so treat this wording as not cleared for reproduction until the renewal status is checked. This is a stricter answer than the record previously gave, and a better-founded one.

author.metaLine: fl. 6th century BCE (traditional) · semi-legendary Chinese sage · reputed author of the Tao Te Ching
author.bio: Lao Tzu (“Old Master,” also romanized Laozi) is the semi-legendary figure traditionally credited with founding philosophical Daoism and composing the Tao Te Ching. Modern scholars regard him as quasi-mythical and the text as a layered compilation reaching its familiar form around the 4th–3rd centuries BCE. The book’s central teaching of wu wei — effortless, non-forcing action in harmony with the Way — is the genuine source of the sentiment behind this popular quote.

misattribution.heading: A real translation, stripped of its translator
misattribution.intro: Not a fabrication. The sentence is a lightly edited line from a published English version of the Tao Te Ching — but it circulates as though Lao Tzu wrote those English words himself, with no translator named.

items.who: Lao Tzu — as though the English words were his own
items.why: The English is Archie J. Bahm’s rendering of ch. 73 — “It does not hurry; yet everything is accomplished” — quoted with “Nature” swapped in for his “It” and his name removed. The Chinese, 繟然而善謀, is given elsewhere as “at ease, and yet good at laying plans” (Lau) or “without haste” (Wu), so “does not hurry” is an ordinary reading of the phrase.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: the passage is genuinely Lao Tzu’s (Tao Te Ching ch. 73), and the English is Archie J. Bahm’s — so quoting it as Lao Tzu’s own words, unattributed to a translator, is the error.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The quote endures because it captures a real and central Daoist intuition: that the natural world produces abundant results without strain, striving, or haste. In the Tao Te Ching, this is the doctrine of wu wei — often translated “non-action” or “effortless action” — the idea that the most effective way to act is to stop forcing and move with the grain of things.

What makes the modern sentence so shareable is that it is smoother and more “productivity”-friendly than most literal renderings — but that smoothness is Bahm’s, not an anonymous internet edit. His “yet everything is accomplished” is itself a free rendering of 善謀, which most translators give as “good at laying plans”. The loss is the translator’s name, not the provenance.
context.detailsSummary: On chapter 73 and the way of heaven
detailsBody: Chapter 73 contrasts two kinds of courage and then describes the way of heaven: it does not contend yet wins, does not speak yet is answered, is not summoned yet comes. The clause behind the quotation is 繟然而善謀 — commonly “at ease, and yet good at laying plans”. Bahm compresses that run into “It does not hurry; yet everything is accomplished”, which is why the popular English sounds more purposeful than the Chinese strictly warrants.
context.pull: The idea is Lao Tzu’s. The sentence is ours — a modern age’s.
